paras: The lynching of Counce O'Neal was the killing of a Black man near Dublin, Georgia, in late November 1882, when a group of men took him from his house at night and riddled his body with bullets. A Macon dispatch said he had been killed for an alleged assault on a little girl and was afterward found to be innocent, while other reports blamed Black neighbors with a grudge.

O'Neal lived about five miles from Dublin, Georgia, in a house the Times-Star called a cabin. His name appeared variously as O'Neill, Counnell, Connece, Counce and Couch O'Neal. According to the Macon dispatch, he had been accused of assaulting a little girl, while a 'Southern Gleanings' item said he had committed 'a criminal offense' several days before his death.

The first wire report said that four men entered his house on a Thursday night, took him out and riddled his body with bullets, though another printing of the same item put the night on Tuesday. The Cincinnati Times-Star, as quoted in Louisiana, described the attackers as 'a mob of masked men' who carried him to the woods and tied him to a tree before shooting him. Other items said he was taken from his bed and that his body was riddled with buckshot.
On December 4 a Macon dispatch reported that O'Neal 'is now found to have been innocent of the crime.' No report of an inquest, arrests or prosecution appears in the coverage.

Only white papers covered the killing, and none of them was published in Georgia. Pennsylvania and Delaware dailies first ran it on November 27 and 28 as a brief crime item headed 'Riddled With Bullets', naming no race for O'Neill and pointing to suspected Black men. A week later the Macon dispatch ran in Washington as 'Innocent Man Lynched' and in Wilmington as 'An Innocent Man Killed', on two successive days in the Wilmington paper.

Southern papers framed the killing differently. The Lake Charles Echo reprinted the Times-Star account but said the paper's politics made it doubt the closing sentence on O'Neal's innocence, which 'looks as if it had been tacked on.' The Austin Statesman called him 'an obnoxious colored man' killed by white men, while a 'Southern Gleanings' column carried in Tennessee and Louisiana said the killing 'was done by negroes.'

Accounts disagreed on who killed O'Neal: the first wire report and the 'Southern Gleanings' item blamed Black men, the Austin Statesman said white men, and the Times-Star named only a masked mob. The motive was likewise given as an old grudge, an alleged assault on a little girl, or an earlier criminal offense, and the date as a Monday, Tuesday or Thursday.

reader.title: Lynching of Counce O'Neal
bases: A group of four or more men took a Black man from his home at night and shot him to death, by one account after tying him to a tree for an alleged assault (A1, A4, A7, A8).

O'Neal was shot to death by four men (A1) or a 'mob of masked men' (A7) with no lawful authority, and the Macon dispatch and Times-Star say he was killed for an alleged assault on a little girl (A4, A7); other items give an old grudge (A1) or a criminal offense (A9) as the motive.
Separate wire and column items (A1, A4, A7, A8, A9) agree that O'Neal was taken from his house near Dublin and shot to death, though they disagree on the date, the killers' race and the motive.

accounts.label: First wire item
accounts.gist: Four men entered O'Neill's house, took him out and riddled him with bullets; some negroes with an old grudge against him were suspected. No race is given for O'Neill.

accounts.label: Macon dispatch
accounts.gist: O'Neal, colored, was tied to a tree and riddled with bullets for an alleged assault on a little girl and was now found to have been innocent.

accounts.label: Cincinnati Times-Star (via Lake Charles Echo)
accounts.gist: A mob of masked men took O'Neal from his cabin to the woods, tied him to a tree and shot him for an alleged criminal assault; his innocence was clearly established. The Echo doubted that last claim.

accounts.label: Austin Statesman item
accounts.gist: O'Neal, 'an obnoxious colored man', was taken from his bed by white men and shot to death.

accounts.label: 'Southern Gleanings' item
accounts.gist: Negroes killed O'Neal with buckshot because he had committed a criminal offense several days before.

framing.detail: Northern dailies ran the first item as a brief crime note headed 'Riddled With Bullets', blaming suspected negroes with a grudge.
The Macon dispatch ran as 'Innocent Man Lynched' and 'An Innocent Man Killed', stressing that the victim was innocent.
The Lake Charles Echo reprinted the Times-Star but said its politics made the innocence sentence look 'tacked on'.
The Austin Statesman called the victim 'an obnoxious colored man' in a one-line roundup item.
The 'Southern Gleanings' item presented the killing as Black men punishing an offense O'Neal 'had committed'.
